# 11-issen: sources

Back-test entry `11-issen.yaml`: Issen, an AI voice tutor for speaking a foreign language (YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2025-06-26, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44387828 (the founders' post and 271 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MIn-issen-your-personalized-ai-voice-language-tutor
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/issen

Status today: same idea ("AI realtime voice companion for language learning", YCC).

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment).**
- "We started this company after struggling to find great tools to practice speaking Japanese and French" (HN).
- The founders' own line that it is not for beginners, honoured in the segment:
  - "So basically if you are starting a new language from zero, then this is not for you?" "That's correct." (HN/44388670, HN/44388778).
  - "Quite honestly our current focus is more for B1+ students" (HN/44388888).
  - "ISSEN is more focused on intermediate and advanced students, and especially those that are willing to use a more difficult app in order to learn faster" (HN/44391572).
- Segment **[author]**, worded from these: "adults in the US learning a foreign language at intermediate level or above, not starting from zero". One CONSUMER role.
- **[author]** The founders are not US-only. US is the default market and nothing public points elsewhere.

**2. What (the job).**
- "We wanted something that would talk with us — realistically, in full conversations — and actually help us improve" (HN).
- Against streaks: apps where users are "achieving long streaks and so on, without actually getting fluent in the language" (HN).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "become able to hold a real conversation in the language".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "Having a tutor can be awesome, but there are downsides: they can be expensive (since you pay by the hour), difficult to schedule, and have a high upfront cost (finding a tutor you like often forces you to cycle through a few that you don’t)" (HN).
- "Human tutors help, but they can be costly, hard to schedule" (YCL, as summarised).
- No time or place is named. **[author]**:
  - Circumstance "they want to practise speaking the language", occasion "practice session", window {7, DAYS}, Frequency 3 to 7 days out of 7, Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80).
  - These are the smallest choice for a daily-habit product, which the founders' "instantly speak and immerse yourself" (HN) implies.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- Intermediate and advanced learners (item 1). YCL addresses people "serious about improving their foreign language skills" (as summarised).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals are the difficulties the thread itself names:
  - vocabulary: the founders' "word bank and SRS flashcards" (HN)
  - understanding natives at speed: HN/44395109's "understanding accents/pronunciations quickly enough"
  - grammar: HN/44395682's "embarrassing holes"
  - finding time: HN/44395109's 2.5 hours a weekday
- The own item, "Finding someone to speak with when it suits", is the founders' scheduling pain in a learner's words.

**5. Who pays.**
- The learner, by subscription: "Pricing: 20 min free trial, $20–29/month" (HN).
- **[author]** Buyer and payer is "Nobody else" only. The founders name no other role. One respondent (Simon Achebe) shows the spouse the thread raises: "I would have a hard time justifying an additional subscription to my wife!" (HN/44389205).

**6. Mechanism.**
- "a custom voice AI pipeline combining STT (speech-to-text), TTS (text-to-speech), LLMs, long term memory, interruptions, turn-taking" (HN).
- "a word bank and SRS flashcards for new words learned in the AI voice chats" (HN).
- "custom curriculums for each student based on goals, interests, and preferences" (HN).
- "works on web, iOS, Android" (HN).
- The `not_assumed` item "the tutor catches pronunciation mistakes" comes from the founder's own answer: "Yes we do have this issue" (HN/44389905).
- Compatibility conditions **[author]**:
  - The tested one, "They could already hold a simple conversation", is the founders' not-for-beginners line, turned into a condition.
  - "speak aloud" draws on HN/44396663, and "steady connection" on HN/44390909 ("it's all server side", HN/44390965).
- Adoption friction **[author]**:
  - The tested effort, "Talk out loud to an AI tutor", is the product's one act.
  - The intro conversation comes from "There is a structured curriculum that gets generated after the intro lesson" (HN/44389578).
- Commitment step **[author]**: "pay for one month after the trial", the first paid act after "20 min free trial" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "$20–29/month (depending on duration and specific geography)" (HN). The founder's price is $20 to $29 a month.
- Tutor cost: "$20/hour on italki on average" (YCL, as summarised; cited there from Glassdoor).
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $80 to $160 a month, is that hourly rate times one to two lessons a week (4 to 8 lessons a month). It is the smallest reading of "you pay by the hour" (HN).
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 36%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- 271 comments, many of them first-person learners. Each respondent below is traced to one.
- The thread also holds the price objection: "I found the pricing and it’s a tough sell! ChatGPT is cheaper." (HN/44389205).
- It holds the trust objection: "I think I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations or errors" (HN/44390451).

## Respondents

- Caleb Nguyen: HN/44388565 (Vietnamese; "I pay $160/mo for Vietnamese tutoring ($20 per class) … I don't have to schedule my classes"). The rescheduling is **[author]**.
- Rosa Delgado-Hart: HN/44391306 ("I currently pay $99 a month to learn Spanish from a live tutor 30 mins a day").
- Patrick Sorensen: HN/44395109 (Thai; "30 minutes every weekday doing flashcards, 45 minutes with a tutor … To save $2,700 a year") and HN/44389181.
- Yuki Brennan: HN/44396663 ("I think I'm around A2 in Japanese … I don't mind texting … but talking just makes me feel very anxious") and HN/44390432 (skipping the textbook's speaking exercises).
- Jin-ho Park: HN/44388971 ("second-gen Korean-American; my korean is weak but conversational"). The call with an aunt is **[author]**.
- Astrid Mallory: HN/44388547 and HN/44388629 (Swedish: "I can have unstructured conversations … in real life here in Sweden", wants "a guided learning experience").
- Derek Holloway: HN/44388976 (ChatGPT voice mode, "pick a random blurb in the news", "an hour long foreign language practice in Spanish while walking my husky"). His $20 a month for ChatGPT is **[author]**.
- Nikos Ferrante: HN/44388531 (Greek "as a beginner … I still got lost 5 minutes in … a long sentence in Greek about how how it is nice to hike in mountains"). He is outside the segment on purpose: beginners reached the real app.
- Laura Pennington (gate No): HN/44388467 ("lost any semblance of proficiency -- mainly because I never have a real occasion to use anything other than English").
- Mateo Lindgren: HN/44388794 ("I used italki extensively and found having a live Columbian tutor invaluable and very affordable … It would genuinely make me sad if those excellent tutors start losing work"). Medellín and $15 are **[author]**.
- Farida Haque: HN/44388539 ("Assimil courses and done lots of comprehensible input … language production is typically the weak point … plenty of lessons on iTalki"). Moving her to French is **[author]**.
- Simon Achebe: HN/44389205 ("Frantastic is absurdly expensive and it made me switch to italki … justifying an additional subscription to my wife").
- Gabriel Stein: HN/44395682 ("living in Buenos Aires for over 18 years … my pronunciations and accent is quite good … a bunch of embarrassing holes").
- Lucía Moreno: HN/44396239 (Chinese "somewhere between HSK 2 and 3 … When I babble … it cuts me off in the first eh"; a native Spanish speaker). The exchange partner is **[author]**.
- Imani Brooks: HN/44396656 ("~Japanese N4, A2 … living outside of Japan, struggle to find good opportunities to output"). Ohio is **[author]**.
- Arjun Kapoor: HN/44390909 ("I do all my language learning on the commuter trains w/o a good connection") and HN/44390855 (Urdu). Urdu as his family's language is **[author]**.
- Tobias Wren (chip): HN/44389852 ("As an intermediate German speaker"). The refusal to say more is an author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person.
- Megan Ashford: HN/44390650 (Russian; "the AI won't spot areas where you e.g. fudge a case ending or the stress on a word").
- Hassan El-Amin (gate No): author's invention, filling a gap. No commenter describes a week without wanting to practise, and a realistic gate needs one in-segment No beside the out-of-practice Laura Pennington.
- Priya Natarajan: HN/44392491 ("I don't think I can trust TTS for language learning. I could be internalizing wrong pronunciation") and HN/44390451 ("I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real person's name.

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** None of the registry's five advantage codes means "available any time". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Speaking practice any time, no tutor to book", because it drops the tutor. `shorter_time` was the other candidate.
- **YC launch wording.** The WebFetch summaries of YCL and YCC were paraphrases, not full text. The two YCL phrases above marked "as summarised" may differ slightly from the page. Every HN quote is verbatim from the thread's API text.
- **Cost estimate.** The $80 to $160 a month is my arithmetic on "$20/hour on italki on average", not a founder statement. Several respondents spend nothing, because the problem's cost to them is the missing practice, not money. So Existing sacrifice is likely to read below the founder's estimate.
- **Market.** US is assumed. Issen prices "depending on duration and specific geography", and nothing public names a US focus.
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/V. Those need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Yuki and Astrid both say words and grammar matter more to them than speaking practice, so as a learner I'd have put them together instead of leaving all four on their own.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and none is grouped.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to idea to paying to sending, but 'Besides the language learner, who has to agree' (14) sits after cost and price, away from the who-decides screens (10–11) it belongs with.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 both ask whether anyone besides the learner decides or agrees to pay. Screens 3 and 4 repeat the same context question.
founder.missing: Nothing asks what learners use today instead and what it costs them. For Issen that means ChatGPT voice mode at about $20 a month and italki tutors at about $20 an hour, which is the real price comparison. Nothing asks about the 20-minute free trial that comes before the first paid month.

PRIMARY.order_why: The flow from missed practice to price to trial makes sense, but the price questions sit under a 'What you do today' label even though they're about Issen, not about what I do now.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 7 both ask what I'd pay for Issen, first as a monthly worth and then as paying for a month after the trial.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what I already use and pay for today. I pay about $160 a month for Vietnamese tutoring at $20 a class, and nobody asked whether scheduling or rescheduling those classes is actually the problem.

screens.why1: Asking whether to collect emails from willing learners fits here, right before the study goes out and just after I named the first real step.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is a B2B word; for a consumer subscription app I'd say early access or a waitlist, though the hint makes the meaning clear.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of learners keen to try Issen is my own call, and I can make it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and both options are plain and distinct.
screens.why5: My first real step was "pay for one month after the trial", but the line strangers see only asks them to leave an email, so the paid commitment drops out.
screens.instead: Ask the people who say yes to try it for real? They'll see: "Would you try a free 20-minute session, then pay for a month if it helps? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions is the natural last step before the study goes out to learners.
screens.why2: The hint packs video, voice, recording once, 400 credits and text-message links into one block, and it says voice while the interviewer is on video, so I had to read it twice to know whether I was choosing a face or a voice.
screens.why3: As the founder of a voice tutor I can judge which voice my learners would want to talk to, from a 5-second sample.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with a preview each, and Daphne already picked, is a complete and distinct choice, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: I chose to lock and record the face Keel preselects, but the screen frames the choice as a voice, so what I picked has drifted from face to voice.
screens.instead: Who should interview your learners on video? Daphne (picked for you) or Saskia; tap to see and hear each. Recording your pick costs 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks learners the questions, it makes sense to choose how they answer before the study goes out, and this is the second-to-last screen.
screens.why2: As a voice-AI founder I read it fine, but the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' and the bare 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' status (is it recording me, or her video?) take a second read.
screens.why3: Whether my B1+ learners should answer by voice or by tapping is a call I can make from knowing them, and I know some, like the anxious A2 speakers, would rather type.
screens.why4: Voice, text, or the learner's choice covers it with no overlap, and each option says plainly what the learner does and when it is ready.
screens.why5: Nothing about Issen or its roles leaks into the format choice, and 'language learners' is my own word for them.
screens.instead: How should language learners answer? — Daphne asks aloud on video (ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap (ready now) / Let them pick when they open the link (ready when Daphne is)

screens.why1: After choosing how learners will answer, picking who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'a search on the Contacts page' refers to a Keel page I have not seen in this flow, so the middle option needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would reach: the learners I already talk to by name, or the HN and language-forum crowd where I would post one link.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the middle option leans on the unexplained 'Contacts page', and the bold labels run straight into their descriptions without a break.
screens.why5: Nothing of Issen's product or roles leaks, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (each gets their own link) / People Keel finds for me (pick a list, Keel makes a link for each) / One open link I post where learners already gather, like a forum or subreddit (each signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside its deciding number, 'Commitment: 4 of 7 said yes', and the Commitment card adds the 5 of 7 bar and '1 short'.
screens.why_b2: The tally of 5 cards over 7 people reads plainly, but the cards skip from 4 to 6, and Existing sacrifice says '4 answered' when 7 answered, so I had to look twice to see what each count is over.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are word for word what I checked, but Existing sacrifice became '8 to 16 hours a month' when my estimate was $80 to $160 a month in tutor money, and Price reads $20 to $30 against my $20 to $29.
screens.why_b4: The only statement explains why one interview asks three parts; nothing says what 4 of 7 on commitment and a price split mean for the $20 to $29 subscription or what to try next.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the miss is not overstated, but Ability to pay's 'Too few to call · 3 of 7 named your price or more' reads as if few answered when it is really a count short of the bar, and nowhere does it say 7 is a small sample.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 7 would pay for a month after the trial (needed 5), and only 3 of 7 put it at $20 or more a month, so price is the likely blocker; test a lower first month or a longer trial with the next people you ask, and remember 7 is a small group.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside a number, but its count line says '4 answered' while the count line below says '7 answered · 4 counted', so the deciding number contradicts the rest of the card.
screens.why_b2: The axis, the median of 4 and my 8-to-16 band are plain, but the strip's '3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)' reads as if 3 people met my bar when only Jin-ho did, and it shows one ghost cell for three people not counted, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: I put the cost at $80 to $160 a month in tutor money, and Keel recast it as hours; the title says learners 'spend' hours while the question and the axis count hours 'missed', which is recognisably my belief but not my words.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say that three of the four counted fall below my low end, or that I need one more counted answer, or how to get one.
screens.why_b5: It rightly calls this a lean on a small group, but '3 of 4' beside 'your bar' softly suggests support the data does not have.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 7 named hours they go without, and 3 of those 4 fall below your 8-hour low (median 4, only Jin-ho reached 8). It leans against you; one more counted answer decides it, so ask the three who named no cost how much practice they missed.

screens.why_b1: The 3 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, 2 short, is right beside the verdict, but the status word 'People disagree' and 'a lean, not a call' never say plainly whether my price belief held, while the stage page already said 'Did not hold'.
screens.why_b2: Price bands with counts, my $20 to $30 marked in its band, 7 people, and the bar at 5 of 7 on the strip are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Price is my dimension, but my price is $20 to $29 a month, and the card turns it into '$20 to $30', a top end I never charge.
screens.why_b4: The So line only sends me to the Insights tab, though the four below-price answers already point at something concrete: three are A2-level or nervous learners and one is happy with a cheap general chatbot, so the question is whether to tighten the segment or the price.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown, the small group is flagged as a lean rather than a call, and a 3-against-4 split is not dressed up as anything stronger.
screens.instead: Not held, leaning: 3 of 7 would pay $20 to $29 a month, 2 short of the bar. The 4 below it are nervous lower-level speakers, a learner who already lives in the language, and one who uses a cheap general chatbot. Check whether the price holds once beginners and chatbot users are left out.

screens.why_b1: 'Too few to call' sits right beside '3 of 7 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know the call and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts where the money comes from over the 3 asked, but its bar '2 of 3' looks met while the card says too few, and I need a second look at the two ghost cells to see the real gate is 5 people at my price.
screens.why_b3: The belief is recognisably mine, but my price was $20 to $29 a month, not $20 to $30, and the 'money they already spend' phrasing is Keel's, not a line I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me to get more people at my price, but it does not say what 3 of 3 paying from existing spend means for Issen, or that 4 of 7 naming less points back at the price.
screens.why_b5: The card keeps n visible (3 answered, 4 not asked because they named less), calls it a small group and 'a lean, not a call', and claims nothing beyond the three tutor-payers.
screens.instead: Lean for you: all 3 who'd pay $20+ (Caleb, Rosa, Patrick) would take it from what they already pay tutors. But 4 of 7 named under $20, so you need 2 more at your price before this counts, and the Price card is the real question.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits directly above '7 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart shows what was counted (who had to agree), over how many (7), and where my bar sits (5 of 7), and all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Buyer and payer' and the line 'The language learner decides, and nobody else has to agree' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it never says what this means for me, such as that I can sell straight to the learner with no household or employer sign-off.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line flags 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so the 7-of-7 result is not oversold, though 'They decide alone on purchases like this' reads a touch general.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean: all 7 paid for something like this on their own, so pitch the learner directly. This does not tell you whether they will pay; Commitment and Price are where the money stage fell short.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside '4 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7 · 1 short', so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the one-month question over 7 people (4 yes, 1 probably not, 2 no), and the marker at 5 shows the bar plainly.
screens.why_b3: The card's belief, 'Most language learners would pay for one month after the trial now.', is word for word the one I checked, and the bar rule matches what Keel set.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that 3 of 7 would not pay and sends me to the Insights tab, so I don't learn here whether to fix the price, the trial length or the target learner.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said, and a miss by one is reported as 1 short rather than a resounding no.
screens.instead: 3 of 7 would not pay after the trial: one is too anxious to speak yet, and two already practise free (ChatGPT voice, real life in Sweden). With 7 people, one more yes would flip this, so test a longer trial or a lower first month before reading it as a no.

screens.why_b1: Both boxes open on their verdict, People disagree and Did not hold, with the deciding count right beside it (3 of 7 at $20 or more, bar 5 of 7, 2 short; 4 of 7 said yes, bar 5 of 7, 1 short).
screens.why_b3: The Commitment belief is my words verbatim, and the Price line's $20 to $30 a month is my $20–29 pricing, close enough that I recognise it at once.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the failed Commitment and the split Price mean for Issen; the Commitment box is empty, and the 'When a line fails' header promises guidance it never gives.
screens.why_b5: The numbers stay visible, but '3 never saw it (Yuki, Astrid, Derek)' reads as if they skipped the commitment question, when they did answer it and only gave their why on the Price line, so the empty Commitment box looks like missing data rather than redirected data.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I did not type: Astrid already speaks every day and is stuck on grammar and vocabulary, not speaking; Yuki is A2 and too anxious to talk, so below my bar; Derek's cheap chatbot voice mode is a direct rival; and Jin-ho would pay more only once it gets them through a whole family call.
screens.instead: Say plainly that the three who would not commit are the same three who gave their why on Price, and show their quotes there; then add the takeaway: two of the four who said no are outside my real target (one is an anxious A2 learner, one already speaks daily and wants grammar), so tighten the segment and test against chatbot voice mode before cutting the price.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's an obvious screener, since the study is about people already past the beginner stage, and I'd expect to be asked my level up front.
screens.why2: "Intermediate" is a word every learner knows, but the question never says which language or what intermediate means, so I'd pause on whether my halting Vietnamese counts.
screens.why3: I know roughly where I stand after paying for tutoring classes, so I can answer this about myself.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, but there's no room for someone like me who can get by in some situations and not others, so a borderline learner would just guess.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's "intermediate level or above", but it drops "a foreign language you're learning" and "not starting from zero", which would have made it clear and concrete; nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and easy to answer yes or no on one hearing, though saying "Yes or no" after it would help.
screens.instead: Are you learning a foreign language and past the beginner stage in it? Yes; No

screens.why1: Right after I confirm I'm intermediate or above, showing me the idea before asking what I think of it makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Words like real-time voice tutor, curriculum and spaced-repetition flashcards are everyday words for someone like me who has used Anki and paid for tutoring, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: It's about practising speaking the language I'm learning, which is exactly what I pay my tutor for, so I can picture it against what I actually do.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: The 'how it works' line is a list of five features rather than one line, and the belief just repeats 'full spoken conversations' and 'not starting from zero' word for word, so the target-group wording appears twice and the card reads like a spec sheet more than an idea.
screens.why6: Said aloud it's a long run of short sentences listing features, with 'spaced-repetition flashcards' as a mouthful and 'not starting a language from zero' heard twice, which is a lot to hold in one listen.
screens.instead: Imagine Issen, a spoken AI language tutor. You talk with it out loud in the language, at your level, about what interests you, and it turns the new words into flashcards for you to review. The people building it believe this would give learners who already know some of the language real conversation practice whenever they want it.

screens.why1: Asking what I give up today fits after the idea card, but it jumps straight to missed hours without first asking whether or how I practise speaking now.
screens.why2: 'Missed' needs a second read: missed against what? My tutor classes are booked and I reschedule rather than skip, so I'm unsure whether it means cancelled classes or practice I wanted and never got.
screens.why3: I know my class hours, but 'hours I missed' is something I'd have to guess, since I never count practice I didn't do.
screens.why4: Three escapes where there should be one, 'I'd rather not say' is not an allowed escape, and 'None' means the same as typing 0 in the box.
screens.why5: The founder's window is the last 7 days but this asks about last month, and 'missed' assumes a planned amount the founder never named.
screens.why6: The stem says well, but 'a number of hours last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful I would not hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, about how many hours did you spend speaking the language with someone? (number of hours; or say I can't recall)

screens.why1: Asking what Issen is worth fits after the idea card, but it sits under a 'What you do today' kicker and comes straight after one question about missed practice hours, so it feels abrupt and mislabelled.
screens.why2: 'What would Issen be worth to you a month' is plain; I'd know straight away what you're asking.
screens.why3: I already pay about $160 a month at $20 a class for tutoring, so I can put a monthly number on a speaking tutor from what I actually spend.
screens.why4: The bands are clean with no overlap, '$100 or more' covers what I pay now, and 'I wouldn't pay for this' plus 'I can't say' are both real and distinct answers.
screens.why5: It's the idea card's own line, a spoken AI language tutor, asked about on purpose, with nothing else of the founder's plan coming through.
screens.why6: The two-step bands are easy to hold by ear, but 'Or say you can't say' trips over itself when spoken.
screens.instead: Kicker 'About the idea'; What would Issen be worth to you a month? Under $10 · $10 to under $20 · $20 to under $50 · $50 to under $100 · $100 or more · I wouldn't pay for this; spoken escape: 'Or say: I can't say.'

screens.why1: Right after I named $20 to $50 a month, asking where that money would come from follows naturally.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself, though 'went ahead at that' is a bit stiff.
screens.why3: I know my budget; I already pay about $160 a month for tutoring, so I can say whether this would come out of that or on top of it.
screens.why4: 'Money I already spend on this' is vague about what 'this' is, and for me it would really be 'instead of some of my tutoring classes', which the wording only hints at.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product or the founder's terms comes through; it just points back to my own price.
screens.why6: Short, with three options I can hold, but 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy aloud, and the spoken stem drops the $20 to $50 the screen shows.
screens.instead: You said about $20 to $50 a month. Where would that come from? From what I pay my tutor now; from other money I'd set aside; or I couldn't pay it. Chip: I can't say

screens.why1: I just said the money comes from my own pocket, so asking whether anyone else had to agree comes close to asking the same thing again, though a family budget could make it fair.
screens.why2: "Something like this" makes me stop and work out whether it means my tutoring, a language app, or the idea I was just shown.
screens.why3: I know exactly who agreed when I signed up for my $20-a-class Vietnamese lessons: nobody but me.
screens.why4: The options jump between yes and no out of order, the two yes options differ only in one person versus several, and "someone else decided for me" is an odd fit for something I pay for myself.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or terms leaks here; it is a plain question about my own payment.
screens.why6: Four short options are easy to hold, but the zig-zag yes-no-yes-no order is hard to follow by ear, and "Or say you can't say" sounds clumsy aloud.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for language lessons, did anyone else have to agree? No, I decided on my own; Yes, one other person agreed; Yes, more than one person agreed. Or say: I can't recall.

screens.why1: Last question after I've said what it's worth and where the money comes from, so asking whether I'd actually pay past the trial is the obvious close, though the 'What you do today' kicker doesn't fit a hypothetical.
screens.why2: Plain words, and trial and paying for a month are how I already think about apps and tutoring.
screens.why3: I know what I spend on my tutor at $20 a class, but I've never tried Issen, and the screen doesn't say what the month would cost, so I'm half guessing.
screens.why4: The yes is firm while the no side gets two options, and 'Probably not' and 'No' sit close together, so there's no room for a hesitant yes like 'Probably, if the trial is good'.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's spoken AI language tutor and its trial reach me, which is what the idea is supposed to show, and nothing else leaks.
screens.why6: Short and one question, but the first option repeats the whole stem back to me and is a mouthful next to the two one-word options.
screens.instead: After the trial, would you pay for a month of Issen at the price you gave? Yes; probably yes; probably not; or no.
